newsitem.title: USA: Soybean, corn, cotton prices fall on plantings estimates.
newsitem.headline: Soybean, corn, cotton prices fall on plantings estimates.

text.p: Prices for corn, soybeans and cotton to be harvested this fall sank on Monday after a government forecast of larger than expected plantings.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, soybeans for delivery in November closed 21 cents a bushel lower at $6.93. Corn for delivery in December ended down 5 cents a bushel at $2.91-1/2.

Prices fell after the Agriculture Department in its first estimate of summer crop seedings said U.S. farmers would plant 68.8 million acres of soybeans, the largest amount in 17 years. Corn plantings were expected at a 12-year high of 81.4 million acres.

Analysts said those plantings and good weather could lead to crops that could challenge the record harvests of 1993. The seedings also overcame caution about tight supplies suggested in another Agriculture Department report issued Monday.

That report put March 1 stocks of soybeans at 1.078 billion bushels, below trade expectations for 1.093 billion and last year's 1.190 billion. Corn stocks of 4.493 billion were also below expectations for 4.565 billion.

Both corn and soybeans, which had good harvests last fall, have seen continuing strong demand from exporters and processors. As a result, corn and soybean futures prices for delivery before the fall harvest were resilient on Monday.
May soybeans closed up 3/4 cent a bushel at $8.55-3/4 and May corn at $3.10, up 1-3/4 cents.

"The market seemed to react more toward the prospects of very large supplies come fall than the very strong demand pace evidenced by the stocks figure," said Joel Karlin, analyst with Everen Securities in Chicago.

"We're talking about exceptionally large, perhaps record corn and soybean crops. But demand for U.S. beans continues to be very strong. Even at these prices, it does not appear to have stifled even domestic demand," Karlin said.
"A lot of people are saying fact or fiction," said grain trader Steve Bruce of E.D. and F. Man International. "Fact are the stocks, and fiction is the acreage."

With planting just under way in the southern United States and farmers given new freedom this year to switch planting choices under the "Freedom to Farm" bill passed last year, analysts said price moves and weather into the spring will remain key to this year's production.
"Farmers can change acreage and they will do so depending on weather," said Terry Francl, senior economist with the American Farm Bureau Federation.
Wheat prices closed lower on market talk that India cancelled a buying tender for 500,000 metric tons. Wheat for May delivery closed 4-1/4 cents a bushel lower at $3.97-1/2.
But traders said the government's estimate of spring wheat plantings at 17.775 million acres was about 775,000 acres below analysts' expectations and should support prices.
At the New York Cotton Exchange, cotton for December delivery closed 1.09 cents a pound lower at 75.35 cents.
The Agriculture Department's estimate for cotton plantings at 14.48 million acres was higher than expectations of 13.7 million to 14.3 million acres.
"We still expect producers to change their plantings, particularly in the face of stronger corn and soybean prices," said Carl Anderson, a cotton marketing specialist with Texas A & M University.

At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, pork prices rose after the Agriculture Department said in its quarterly pig crop report Friday that the number of hogs kept for market on U.S. farms on March 1 was down 475,000 animals from a year ago.
June hogs rose 0.85 cent a pound to 81.875 cents and May pork bellies closed up 2.925 cents a pound at 78.050 cents.

Traders cited continuing optimism about a large pickup in pork exports as another factor fueling buying after Taiwan halted pork exports this month due to a severe outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in its hog herd.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, gasoline futures led the oil complex mostly lower in light volume and the expiry of the April refined products contracts.
Unleaded gasoline for delivery in April closed down 0.95 at 63.68 cents a gallon and April crude oil closed down 29 cents at $20.41 a barrel.
April heating oil, aided by a cold snap on the East Coast, ended 0.65 cent a gallon higher at 56.72 cents.
"It was pretty much a quiet day," said Tom Bentz, of ING Derivatives Clearing Inc.
